en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Familiarity from the Book of Puzzles (Meṇḍakapañha)
1. The Question on Familiarity “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘From familiarity fear is born;’”
“Dust arises from having a home;
for one who is homeless and without attachment—
this indeed is the vision of a sage.”
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One:
“One should cause delightful monasteries to be built; one should dwell there with those who are learned.
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was indeed said by the Tathāgata—
“‘Fear arises from intimacy; dust is born from a home.

To be homeless and without intimacy—this indeed is the vision of a sage. Therefore, as for the statement, ‘One should have pleasant monasteries built and dwell there with those of great learning,’ that is false, if it was spoken by the Tathāgata.”
“If it is said, ‘One should have a delightful monastery built; one should dwell there with those who are learned,’ then the statement, ‘Fear arises from intimacy; dust is born from a home.
Homelessness and lack of intimacy—this indeed is the vision of a sage,’ would be false.
This too is a dilemma from both sides that has come upon you; it must be resolved by you.”
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Fear arises from intimacy; dust is born from a home.
To be homeless and without intimacy—this, truly, is the vision of a sage.’”
And it was said:
“One should cause delightful monasteries to be built; there one should lodge those who are learned.
This, O Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One.
“‘From intimacy fear is born; from a home dust arises.

Homelessness and non-intimacy—this indeed is the vision of a sage. This is a statement of its true nature, a complete statement, an exhaustive statement, a literal statement—one that is fitting for a recluse, appropriate for a recluse, resembling a recluse, worthy of a recluse, and the proper domain of a recluse.
The way of the recluse, the practice of the recluse.
Just as, O Great King, a forest deer wandering in the forest wilds sleeps wherever he wishes, without a home and without a dwelling;
even so, O Great King, should a bhikkhu [reflect]: "Fear arises from intimacy; from a dwelling arises dust."
"One should reflect: 'Homelessness and lack of intimacy—this indeed is the vision of a sage.

Furthermore, Great King, as for that which was spoken by the Blessed One—"One should cause delightful monasteries to be built; one should dwell there with those of great learning"—that was spoken by the Blessed One while considering two purposes.
Which two?
The gift of a monastery is praised, approved, extolled, and lauded by all Buddhas; by giving that gift of a monastery, they will be liberated from birth, aging, and death.
This, first of all, is the benefit in the gift of a monastery.

Furthermore, while a monastery exists, the bhikkhunīs will have a well-established convention; they will be easy to see for those who wish to see them, whereas in the absence of a fixed residence, they will be difficult to see.
This is the second benefit in the gift of a monastery.
Seeing these two purposes, the Blessed One said:
"One should cause delightful monasteries to be built and dwell there with those who are learned"—yet a son of the Buddha should not form an attachment to such a dwelling place.
"Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.
Thus ends the first question on intimacy.
